catalog_quote: Kanuri is a tone language. Tone is of great importance in Kanuri, both lexically and grammatically. ... Synchronic Kanuri has certain of the characteristics of a nonrestricted (lexical) tone language, as well as certain characteristics typical of a restricted (tone harmony) language. ... All of the tone patterns of Fanuri words are based in a two-tone system, a level high (F) tone, and a level low (L) tone. In both diachronic and synchronic word formation processes, these level syllabic tones may combine over a given syllable to result in combined or contour tones, the combination H-L resulting in a falling (F) tone, the combination L-H resulting in a rising (R) tome. ... Because a language is tonal does not mean that it is sung. It means rather that every syllable has a designated pitch, relative to the pitch of the other syllables 'in a word, compound, or combination of words. ... The…

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the standard 363-pp reference grammar of Yerwa Kanuri (Hutchison 1981), which we hold as a full scanned text; the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are both present verbatim at the stated chapters/pages, and a whole-grammar grep by the original readers (re-checked here at the cited lines) shows 'stress' used only for phrase-level emphasis and explicitly denied as the marker of compounding. Glottolog lists nothing later and weightier on phonology; web search turned up no instrumental/prosody study and no competing stress analysis, and the two open items fetched sources today (Hutchison's ALMA introduction; Gombe 2019 citing Bulakarima & Shettima 2012) both restate Kanuri as a tone language with H/L plus contour (and mid) tones. sources.citation: Hutchison, John P. [n.d., uploaded 2023]. Introduction to the Kanuri Language. African Language Materials Archive (ALMA), Michigan State University, 26 pp. https://alma.matrix.msu.edu/assets/uploads/2023/02/
sources.quote: 'Tone is not indicated in the SKO. For the purposes of this introduction, we have included only the high tone (marked by the acute accent) marks and some falling tones marked by the circumflex. Syllables without tone markings are low tones.' Word formation listed as 'affixation, tone change, epenthesis, and reduplication' (e.g. Kanúri vs Kanurí by tone change). No word stress mentioned.

sources.quote: 'Both languages are tone languages: While Kanuri has five tones (high, low, rising, falling and mid), Hausa has only three tones (high, low and falling).' Secondary, attributed to Bulakarima & Shettima (2012) A sketch of Kanuri phonology and tone.

sources.citation: Koelle, Sigismund Wilhelm. 1854. Grammar of the Bornu or Kanuri Language. London: Church Missionary House. archive.org item grammarofbrnuo00koelrich (scanned text).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage 2235.54; FIG HathiTrust (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.quote: Pre-tonal 19th-century description from one displaced speaker in Sierra Leone: 'The accented syllable is indicated by the acute accent'; diphthongs 'when they receive the accent, it is always placed on the last of the two vowels'; syllabic nasals may be 'even assuming the accent of the word'. Koelle himself flags his informant as 'a little uncertain' on 'the quantity of the vowels and the accent'. No tone analysis; superseded by Lukas 1937 and Hutchison 1981, so it does not bear on the tonal coding.
